bull_bear.body:
- Licensed use of the long-standing 'Vithal Kamats' / 'Kamats' trade marks and copyrights, giving brand recognition without owning the marks
- Asset-light franchising model - the Company develops operating systems and grants franchises under trade marks to dine-in and kiosk operators
- Standardised, hygienic quick-serve menu replicated across highway and city outlets
- Multi-format brand stable spanning quick-serve (Vithal Kamats/Kamats), themed casual dining (Urban Dhaba), multi-cuisine (Pepper Fry) and premium South Indian (Kamats Legacy)
- Kamats Hospitality Academy of Skill (KHAS), an in-house initiative addressing the shortage of skilled hospitality labour by training and employing youth
- Vertical extension into owned hotel rooms (Silvassa) and a subsidiary-led hotel development (Nani Daman) alongside the restaurant base
bull_bear.title: Bull — competitive strengths

bull_bear.body:
- Demand is tied to discretionary consumer spending — MD&A: 'As the industry remains closely linked to discretionary consumer spending, any adverse economic developments may impact demand and operating performance.' Hotel and restaurant volumes therefore swing with the consumption cycle rather than with contracted demand.
- Input-cost inflation - manpower, utilities and food — MD&A Threats, Risks and concerns explicitly names 'inflationary pressures, rising manpower, utility and food costs'. These are the dominant operating costs of a restaurant and hotel chain and are hard to pass on quickly in a value/mid-market format.
- Changing consumer preferences — Flagged in the MD&A risk paragraph. The Company's formats are standardised quick-serve, themed dhaba, multi-cuisine and premium South Indian dining; a shift in dining preference directly affects footfall across the licensed brand portfolio.
- Rising competitive intensity in hospitality and organised dining — Named in the MD&A risk paragraph; the same MD&A notes the restaurant segment is expanding on organised dining, premiumisation and technology-enabled delivery platforms, i.e. the industry is drawing in competition and new channels.
- Regulatory change, including tax and food-safety regulation — MD&A names 'regulatory changes' as a risk, and the year's key policy development was the 56th GST Council rationalisation effective 22 September 2025 (5% GST without ITC on room tariffs up to Rs.7,500/day). The Secretarial Audit also lists the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006 and the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954 as laws specifically applicable to the Company.
- Single-segment / single-industry concentration — MD&A: 'The Company is presently operational in only one segment i.e. hospitality, food products and allied activities.' There is no diversifying business line to offset a hospitality downturn.
- Execution and ramp-up risk on new outlets and hotel projects — The Board's Report states 'Profit before tax was registered low due to initial operating cost of new outlets.' Two projects are still to land - the Urban Dhaba (Urban Bar) restaurant at Bhandup expected to commence by July 2026 and the subsidiary's ~100-room Nani Daman hotel targeted for the coming financial year - so near-term earnings carry start-up drag and completion risk.
- Availability of skilled hospitality labour — The Board's Report describes the Kamats Hospitality Academy of Skill (KHAS) as an initiative 'to address the concern of skilled labour', i.e. management itself identifies skilled-manpower scarcity as a constraint on a business it also calls manpower-dependent (171 employees on the payroll as on 31 March 2026).
- Global economic and geopolitical uncertainty — Named first in the MD&A risk paragraph alongside supply-chain disruption and evolving international trade dynamics; it feeds through to inbound tourism and business travel demand.
bull_bear.title: Bear — key risks

business.body: The Company is in the business of hospitality, food products and allied activities, running a chain of restaurants serving hygienic standardised food items in a quick-serve format at outlets on national highways, state highways and in cities. Its business model is to develop the operating systems and grant franchises under trade marks to restaurant chains operating in dine-in and kiosk formats; the Company does not own the brands 'Vithal Kamats', 'Kamats' and others and has licensed them from their respective owners. Alongside restaurants it operates hotel rooms (Silvassa) and, through its subsidiary Vitizen Hotels Limited, is developing a hotel property at Nani Daman.

outlook.body:
- Enhance operational efficiencies and deliver superior guest experiences while maintaining prudent financial discipline
- Strengthen both the hotel and the restaurant offerings, i.e. build the owned/managed rooms business alongside the franchised restaurant chain
- Leverage digital technologies and technology-led customer engagement
- Expand into emerging cities and leisure destinations as a source of long-term value creation
- Grow the franchising model - develop operating systems and grant franchises under licensed trade marks (Vithal Kamats/Kamats, Urban Dhaba, Pepper Fry) for dine-in and kiosk formats
- Add hotel room inventory through the subsidiary Vitizen Hotels Limited, which is building a ~100-room property at Nani Daman expected to contribute significantly to consolidated revenue and regional presence
- Evaluate further development and expansion of additional rooms at the Silvassa property, contingent upon market suitability, demand and operational viability
- Address the shortage of skilled hospitality labour in-house through the Kamats Hospitality Academy of Skill (KHAS), which trains youth and employs them
- Groom in-house talent to take higher responsibilities (manpower described as the Company's biggest strength)
outlook.title: Strategy & capital allocation

outlook.body: FY26 expansion was concentrated in three named projects. At the Silvassa property the Company developed and commenced full commercial operations for a total of 99 guest rooms, adding to the existing 75 rooms; management says it plans to evaluate further development and expansion of additional rooms at this location in future, contingent upon market suitability, demand and operational viability. In Mumbai, the Company acquired Shop Nos. 7, 8, 17, 20 and 21 at Bhandup on long-term lease and has successfully completed refurbishment and interior fit-outs of the combined premises, which will operate as a premium dining establishment under the brand 'Urban Dhaba (Urban Bar) Restaurants', expected to commence by July 2026. Through its subsidiary Vitizen Hotels Limited, the Company has commenced full-scale construction and development of a ~100-room hotel property at Kavi Khabardar Marg, Main Road, Near Jetti, Nani Daman; construction and fit-out are in full swing and the project is on track to commence operations in the coming financial year, and on becoming operational is expected to contribute significantly to consolidated revenue and to market presence in the region. Profit before tax for the year was held back by the initial operating cost of new outlets. Proceeds from the warrant issue / converted equity shares are being used for the purposes disclosed in the offer documents with no deviation. The Company also runs the Kamats Hospitality Academy of Skill (KHAS) to train and employ youth and address the shortage of skilled hospitality labour. No rupee capex programme or spend target is stated in the narrative chapters.
outlook.title: Capex & expansion plans

outlook.body:
- Indian hospitality industry outlook remains positive, supported by favourable demographics, rising disposable incomes, increasing domestic and international tourism, improving aviation and tourism infrastructure and continued government initiatives
- Demand expected to remain broad-based across leisure, business travel, MICE, destination weddings and religious tourism
- FY26 industry growth was driven by robust domestic tourism, increasing business travel, growth in leisure and religious tourism, rising disposable incomes and sustained investment in tourism infrastructure; healthy occupancy levels and improved average room rates supported performance
- Restaurant segment expanding on changing consumer preferences, organised dining, premiumisation and technology-enabled food delivery platforms
- GST rationalisation from the 56th GST Council Meeting effective 22 September 2025 - room tariffs up to Rs.7,500 per day now at 5% GST without ITC - expected to improve affordability and stimulate demand in the mid-market hospitality segment
- Macro backdrop: Economic Survey projects real GDP growth of 6.8% to 7.2% for FY 2026-27, with inflation moderating and domestic consumption resilient
- Watch-item: demand is closely linked to discretionary consumer spending; inflationary pressure on manpower, utility and food costs, regulatory change and rising competitive intensity are the flagged threats
- FY26 profit before tax was held back by the initial operating cost of new outlets

risks.risk: Demand is tied to discretionary consumer spending
risks.note: MD&A: 'As the industry remains closely linked to discretionary consumer spending, any adverse economic developments may impact demand and operating performance.' Hotel and restaurant volumes therefore swing with the consumption cycle rather than with contracted demand.

risks.risk: Input-cost inflation - manpower, utilities and food
risks.note: MD&A Threats, Risks and concerns explicitly names 'inflationary pressures, rising manpower, utility and food costs'. These are the dominant operating costs of a restaurant and hotel chain and are hard to pass on quickly in a value/mid-market format.

Flagged in the MD&A risk paragraph. The Company's formats are standardised quick-serve, themed dhaba, multi-cuisine and premium South Indian dining; a shift in dining preference directly affects footfall across the licensed brand portfolio.

risks.risk: Rising competitive intensity in hospitality and organised dining
risks.note: Named in the MD&A risk paragraph; the same MD&A notes the restaurant segment is expanding on organised dining, premiumisation and technology-enabled delivery platforms, i.e. the industry is drawing in competition and new channels.

risks.risk: Regulatory change, including tax and food-safety regulation
risks.note: MD&A names 'regulatory changes' as a risk, and the year's key policy development was the 56th GST Council rationalisation effective 22 September 2025 (5% GST without ITC on room tariffs up to Rs.7,500/day). The Secretarial Audit also lists the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006 and the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954 as laws specifically applicable to the Company.
MD&A: 'The Company is presently operational in only one segment i.e. hospitality, food products and allied activities.' There is no diversifying business line to offset a hospitality downturn.

risks.risk: Execution and ramp-up risk on new outlets and hotel projects
risks.note: The Board's Report states 'Profit before tax was registered low due to initial operating cost of new outlets.' Two projects are still to land - the Urban Dhaba (Urban Bar) restaurant at Bhandup expected to commence by July 2026 and the subsidiary's ~100-room Nani Daman hotel targeted for the coming financial year - so near-term earnings carry start-up drag and completion risk.

The Board's Report describes the Kamats Hospitality Academy of Skill (KHAS) as an initiative 'to address the concern of skilled labour', i.e. management itself identifies skilled-manpower scarcity as a constraint on a business it also calls manpower-dependent (171 employees on the payroll as on 31 March 2026).
Named first in the MD&A risk paragraph alongside supply-chain disruption and evolving international trade dynamics; it feeds through to inbound tourism and business travel demand.

one_liner.title: One Liner (RHP)
one_liner.body: Vikram Kamats Hospitality Limited (formerly Vidli Restaurants Limited) operates and franchises a chain of standardised quick-service and dine-in restaurants under licensed 'Vithal Kamats'/'Kamats' brands while building an owned hotel portfolio, working in a single segment of hospitality, food …

business_model.title: What they do
business_model.body: The Company is in the business of hospitality, food products and allied activities, running a chain of restaurants serving hygienic standardised food items in a quick-serve format at outlets on national highways, state highways and in cities. Its business model is to develop the operating systems and grant franchises under trade marks to restaurant chains operating in dine-in and kiosk formats; the Company does not own the brands 'Vithal Kamats', 'Kamats' and others and has licensed them from their respective owners. Alongside restaurants it operates hotel rooms (Silvassa) and, through its subsidiary Vitizen Hotels Limited, is developing a hotel property at Nani Daman.

group_structure.title: Group structure (subsidiaries / JV / related parties)
group_structure.body:
- Vitizen Hotels Limited — subsidiary: Sole subsidiary, 84.01% shareholding, subsidiary since 29 March 2022; reporting period ended 31/03/2026; no proposed dividend. Hotel operator - developing a ~100-room property at Nani Daman; also appointed as agent of the Company to collect royalty/fees from franchisees and operates/manages the hotel and restaurant units at Silvassa.
- Kamat Holiday Resorts (Silvassa) Limited — associate: Named in the Ind AS 24 related-party roster; sits under the heading 'Associate Company where control exists and Transaction have taken place during the year'. Transactions listed include security deposit given on lease of shop, lease rent and co-borrower arrangements in respect of secured borrowing.
- VITS Hospitality Co. Ltd. / Vits Hospitality Company Ltd — associate: Described in the related-party note as an associate of the subsidiary
- Vits Hotels Worldwide Pvt. Ltd. — related party: Group hospitality entity in the Ind AS 24 roster - company in which directors are common / members

products.title: Products & brands
products.body: - **Hospitality, food products and allied activities:** Vithal Kamats / Kamats (franchised trade mark, quick-serve and dine-in), Urban Dhaba - The Rich Taste of Punjab (Punjabi dhaba theme, Indian/North Indian veg and non-veg, live music and live bar), Pepper Fry Veg Multi-Cuisine Kitchen - by Kamats (multi-cuisine restaurant), Kamats Legacy (premium South Indian dining, four outlets), Urban Dhaba (Urban Bar) Restaurants (premium dining, Bhandup - yet to commence), Hotel rooms (Silvassa property)

end_markets.title: End Markets (RHP)
end_markets.body:
- India - domestic hospitality and organised dining
- Highway travellers (outlets on national and state highways)
- Urban dining, Mumbai / Navi Mumbai / Thane (Nariman Point, Vashi, Malad, Mira Road, Bhandup)
- Silvassa (hotel rooms)
- Nani Daman (hotel under construction via subsidiary)
- Domestic tourism, business travel, leisure and religious tourism, MICE and destination weddings (industry demand drivers cited in MD&A)

demand_drivers.title: Demand & outlook drivers
demand_drivers.body:
- Indian hospitality industry outlook remains positive, supported by favourable demographics, rising disposable incomes, increasing domestic and international tourism, improving aviation and tourism infrastructure and continued government initiatives
- Demand expected to remain broad-based across leisure, business travel, MICE, destination weddings and religious tourism
- FY26 industry growth was driven by robust domestic tourism, increasing business travel, growth in leisure and religious tourism, rising disposable incomes and sustained investment in tourism infrastructure; healthy occupancy levels and improved average room rates supported performance
- Restaurant segment expanding on changing consumer preferences, organised dining, premiumisation and technology-enabled food delivery platforms
- GST rationalisation from the 56th GST Council Meeting effective 22 September 2025 - room tariffs up to Rs.7,500 per day now at 5% GST without ITC - expected to improve affordability and stimulate demand in the mid-market hospitality segment
- Macro backdrop: Economic Survey projects real GDP growth of 6.8% to 7.2% for FY 2026-27, with inflation moderating and domestic consumption resilient
- Watch-item: demand is closely linked to discretionary consumer spending; inflationary pressure on manpower, utility and food costs, regulatory change and rising competitive intensity are the flagged threats
- FY26 profit before tax was held back by the initial operating cost of new outlets

capital_allocation.title: Strategy & capital allocation
capital_allocation.body:
- Enhance operational efficiencies and deliver superior guest experiences while maintaining prudent financial discipline
- Strengthen both the hotel and the restaurant offerings, i.e. build the owned/managed rooms business alongside the franchised restaurant chain
- Leverage digital technologies and technology-led customer engagement
- Expand into emerging cities and leisure destinations as a source of long-term value creation
- Grow the franchising model - develop operating systems and grant franchises under licensed trade marks (Vithal Kamats/Kamats, Urban Dhaba, Pepper Fry) for dine-in and kiosk formats
- Add hotel room inventory through the subsidiary Vitizen Hotels Limited, which is building a ~100-room property at Nani Daman expected to contribute significantly to consolidated revenue and regional presence
- Evaluate further development and expansion of additional rooms at the Silvassa property, contingent upon market suitability, demand and operational viability
- Address the shortage of skilled hospitality labour in-house through the Kamats Hospitality Academy of Skill (KHAS), which trains youth and employs them
- Groom in-house talent to take higher responsibilities (manpower described as the Company's biggest strength)

moat.title: Bull — competitive strengths
moat.body:
- Licensed use of the long-standing 'Vithal Kamats' / 'Kamats' trade marks and copyrights, giving brand recognition without owning the marks
- Asset-light franchising model - the Company develops operating systems and grants franchises under trade marks to dine-in and kiosk operators
- Standardised, hygienic quick-serve menu replicated across highway and city outlets
- Multi-format brand stable spanning quick-serve (Vithal Kamats/Kamats), themed casual dining (Urban Dhaba), multi-cuisine (Pepper Fry) and premium South Indian (Kamats Legacy)
- Kamats Hospitality Academy of Skill (KHAS), an in-house initiative addressing the shortage of skilled hospitality labour by training and employing youth

risks.title: Bear — key risks
risks.body:
- Demand is tied to discretionary consumer spending — MD&A: 'As the industry remains closely linked to discretionary consumer spending, any adverse economic developments may impact demand and operating performance.' Hotel and restaurant volumes therefore swing with the consumption cycle rather than with contracted demand.
- Input-cost inflation - manpower, utilities and food — MD&A Threats, Risks and concerns explicitly names 'inflationary pressures, rising manpower, utility and food costs'. These are the dominant operating costs of a restaurant and hotel chain and are hard to pass on quickly in a value/mid-market format.
- Changing consumer preferences — Flagged in the MD&A risk paragraph. The Company's formats are standardised quick-serve, themed dhaba, multi-cuisine and premium South Indian dining; a shift in dining preference directly affects footfall across the licensed brand portfolio.
- Rising competitive intensity in hospitality and organised dining — Named in the MD&A risk paragraph; the same MD&A notes the restaurant segment is expanding on organised dining, premiumisation and technology-enabled delivery platforms, i.e. the industry is drawing in competition and new channels.
- Regulatory change, including tax and food-safety regulation — MD&A names 'regulatory changes' as a risk, and the year's key policy development was the 56th GST Council rationalisation effective 22 September 2025 (5% GST without ITC on room tariffs up to Rs.7,500/day). The Secretarial Audit also lists the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006 and the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954 as laws specifically applicable to the Company.
- Single-segment / single-industry concentration — MD&A: 'The Company is presently operational in only one segment i.e. hospitality, food products and allied activities.' There is no diversifying business line to offset a hospitality downturn.
- Execution and ramp-up risk on new outlets and hotel projects — The Board's Report states 'Profit before tax was registered low due to initial operating cost of new outlets.' Two projects are still to land - the Urban Dhaba (Urban Bar) restaurant at Bhandup expected to commence by July 2026 and the subsidiary's ~100-room Nani Daman hotel targeted for the coming financial year - so near-term earnings carry start-up drag and completion risk.
- Availability of skilled hospitality labour — The Board's Report describes the Kamats Hospitality Academy of Skill (KHAS) as an initiative 'to address the concern of skilled labour', i.e. management itself identifies skilled-manpower scarcity as a constraint on a business it also calls manpower-dependent (171 employees on the payroll as on 31 March 2026).
- Global economic and geopolitical uncertainty — Named first in the MD&A risk paragraph alongside supply-chain disruption and evolving international trade dynamics; it feeds through to inbound tourism and business travel demand.
